domains.name: Academic Vocabulary
domains.summary: Academic Vocabulary covers the lexical platform for university study: the vocabulary size and text coverage needed to read and listen independently; the general academic, sub-technical and technical layers of university lexis; the word-level knowledge (morphology, word grammar, countability, spelling) needed for accurate production; and the strategies learners use to keep expanding vocabulary beyond the classroom. Academic word lists (AWL, AVL) are treated as useful but contested starting points, because the 'academic' status, meaning and frequency of items vary by discipline, and coverage thresholds are treated as approximate planning guides rather than cut-offs.
domains.learnerSummary: You will learn which words are most worth your time for university study, how to learn and remember them efficiently, and how to use them accurately and precisely in your own writing and speaking.

stageEmphasis.foundation: Secure the high-frequency base, word families and the vocabulary of university study and assignments, and establish independent learning routines with dictionaries and word cards.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional: Build general academic vocabulary with its word grammar and collocations, set realistic size goals from coverage research, and practise inferring and checking meaning from context.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-ug: Move academic and sub-technical vocabulary into accurate productive use within the student's discipline, including process verbs, evaluative lexis and discipline-specific senses.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-pgt: Prioritise disciplinary terminology, lexical precision and evaluation for source-based writing on compressed one-year programmes.
stageEmphasis.pgr: Refine precision, shell nouns and evaluative lexis for research writing, using evidence from the target field's literature.

domains.name: Phraseology & Formulaic Language
domains.summary: Phraseology & Formulaic Language treats multi-word units — collocations, lexical bundles, spoken formulas and fixed expressions — as core carriers of academic meaning rather than decorative extras. Corpus research shows that expert academic writing and speech rely heavily on recurrent combinations whose functions differ (research-, text- and stance-oriented) and vary by discipline, and that L2 and novice writers tend to underuse, misuse or overuse them. The domain also develops strategies (corpus consultation, critical use of phrase resources) so that learners can verify phraseology independently, while guarding against formulaic, template-driven text.
domains.learnerSummary: You will learn to notice and use the word combinations that academic writers and lecturers rely on, and to check combinations yourself with corpus tools (searchable collections of real academic texts) and phrase resources without filling your writing with stock phrases.

stageEmphasis.foundation: Build the habit of noticing and recording combinations, with frequent academic collocations and text-organising bundles from course materials.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional: Extend collocational range, introduce research- and stance-oriented bundles linked to calibration, and train learners in collocation dictionaries, simple corpus searches and critical phrasebank use.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-ug: Work on learners' own drafts: repair persistent miscollocations, reduce overused connectors and stance frames, and compare bundles with those in disciplinary texts.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-pgt: Prioritise discipline-relevant collocations and bundles for source-based writing, checked against field texts in a compressed timeframe.
stageEmphasis.pgr: Profile the phraseology of target journals with self-built corpora and refine stance formulas for research writing and publication.

domains.name: Register & Academic Style
domains.summary: Register & Academic Style develops learners' ability to read a communicative situation and choose language accordingly: register as a configuration of field, tenor and mode; the systematic differences in how speech and writing package meaning; and the features conventionally associated with formal academic prose. The domain deliberately treats style 'rules' as probabilistic tendencies to be tested against evidence of disciplinary and historical variation, frames impersonality as a choice about agency rather than a route to objectivity, and extends to inclusive language and to writing for non-specialist readers.
domains.learnerSummary: You will learn why academic writing and speech sound the way they do, how to adjust your style for different readers, purposes and disciplines, and how to tell real conventions from over-simplified 'rules'.

stageEmphasis.foundation: Build register awareness through concrete contrasts (email, forum post, assignment) and an explicit, reasoned checklist of formality features, including precise rather than vague reference.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional: Make spoken–written differences and formality choices explicit tools for reading-into-writing and presentations, and begin testing prescriptive style rules against exemplars.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-ug: Reconcile conflicting module advice by examining disciplinary style, authorial presence and density in the student's own field and genres.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-pgt: Calibrate density, impersonality and inclusive description for compressed source-based and professional writing, often in an unfamiliar discipline.
stageEmphasis.pgr: Align style with target journals and examiners' fields, claim contribution with appropriate presence, and write lay summaries and engagement texts for non-specialists.

domains.name: Academic Grammar
domains.summary: This domain covers the grammatical resources that carry meaning in academic registers, prioritised by what corpus research shows academic writing actually does rather than by a general-English syllabus order. Its centre of gravity is the noun phrase: academic prose compresses information into premodified and postmodified noun phrases and nominalisations far more than conversation does, so learners need both to unpack such phrases when reading and to build them when writing. Clause-level resources (tense, voice, modality, subordination, complement and reporting clauses) are treated in terms of the rhetorical choices they serve, such as currency in citation, agency in methods and degrees of commitment in claims. Accuracy topics are framed as monitoring and editing problems as much as knowledge problems.
domains.learnerSummary: You will learn the grammar that academic texts rely on most, especially how long noun phrases pack information, and how choices of tense, voice and sentence structure change what your writing claims. You will also build routines for finding and fixing your own most frequent errors.

stageEmphasis.foundation: Secure clause analysis, agreement, articles, tense and basic subordination with textbook-level texts, and introduce noun-phrase expansion through description and definition tasks.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional: Shift attention from clause-combining to phrasal complexity, tense and voice in source-based writing, reporting structures and personal error monitoring tied to the progression assignment.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-ug: Address grammar through students' disciplinary reading and assessed drafts, focusing on noun phrases, reporting, passive versus active choices and recurrent errors flagged in feedback.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-pgt: Concentrate on nominalisation, tense in literature reviews, stance-bearing structures and editing efficiency under the time pressure of a one-year programme.
stageEmphasis.pgr: Refine information packaging (clefts, fronting, end-weight), voice and tense choices in research genres and independent self-editing for publication.

domains.name: Sentence Construction & Punctuation
domains.summary: This domain covers how clauses are combined into well-formed sentences, how punctuation marks grammatical structure and meaning, and how sentence-level choices (length, concision, end-weight) affect readability. Punctuation is treated as a consequence of clause and phrase analysis rather than as a list of rules, and conventions that vary by style guide (serial commas, quotation marks, capitalisation, numbers) are taught as choices to be applied consistently. Sentence-level style is grounded in what corpus research shows about academic prose, in particular that its difficulty comes mainly from dense noun phrases rather than from long chains of clauses.
domains.learnerSummary: You will learn to build clear, correctly punctuated sentences and to apply the conventions your department or style guide expects. You will also learn to edit sentences so that readers can follow dense academic ideas easily.

stageEmphasis.foundation: Establish sentence types, boundaries, core comma and capitalisation conventions, and basic number and list formatting in short assignments.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional: Consolidate boundary and punctuation accuracy under time pressure, introduce semicolons, colons, quotation punctuation and concision for word-limited progression tasks.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-ug: Address style-guide conventions required by departments and sentence-level clarity in assessed reports and essays.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-pgt: Focus on concision, end-weight and consistent application of a style guide in dissertations and data-heavy writing.
stageEmphasis.pgr: Refine sentence-level clarity, end-weight and house-style conventions for theses and journal submission.

domains.name: Cohesion & Coherence
domains.summary: This domain covers the resources that make a text hang together for its reader: cohesive ties (reference, conjunction, lexical cohesion) and the information-structuring choices (given–new order, thematic progression, encapsulation, text patterns) that make a sequence of sentences read as a purposeful whole. It treats cohesion as a means to coherence rather than a proxy for it, countering the connector-heavy, checklist approach that learner-corpus findings and test preparation tend to reinforce. Topics move from sentence-to-sentence linking towards text-level signalling and the reader-oriented expectations of English-medium academic writing, including spoken signposting in lectures and presentations.
domains.learnerSummary: You will learn how writers and speakers help their audience follow their thinking — by linking sentences, keeping key terms consistent, putting familiar information first and signalling where a text is going — and why adding more linking words does not by itself make writing clear.

stageEmphasis.foundation: Foundation programmes concentrate on basic connectors, pronoun and noun reference, paragraph-level patterns and signposting in lectures, using short model texts and subject textbooks.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional: Pre-sessional courses move learners from connector lists to information flow, encapsulation and reverse outlining for coherence in extended source-based writing.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-ug: Undergraduate in-sessional work diagnoses coherence problems in students' own assignments, especially reliance on connectors, unclear reference and weak transitions between paragraphs.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-pgt: Taught postgraduate support focuses on dissertation-length coherence, terminological consistency and transitions between sections, and on using text patterns to read efficiently.
stageEmphasis.pgr: Doctoral writers refine flow in dense prose (thematic progression, encapsulation) and manage metatext and terminology across a thesis or article.

domains.name: Stance, Metadiscourse & Evaluation
domains.summary: This domain covers the interpersonal dimension of academic discourse: how writers and speakers signal certainty and commitment, evaluate ideas and sources, represent themselves, engage readers, and keep their own claims distinct from those they attribute to others. It draws on Hyland's models of metadiscourse and of stance and engagement and on Martin and White's appraisal framework, especially engagement, treating them as complementary lenses rather than a single taxonomy. Stance is approached as calibration and positioning grounded in evidence, not as lists of hedges to insert, and disciplinary variation is made explicit throughout.
domains.learnerSummary: You will learn how to show how sure you are about a claim and how to evaluate other people's work fairly. You will also learn when and how to make your own voice heard, and how to show the reader which ideas are yours and which come from your sources.

stageEmphasis.foundation: Foundation programmes introduce basic hedging and boosting, qualified generalisations and simple opinion language in speech and writing, linked to avoiding sweeping claims.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional: Pre-sessional courses develop calibration of claims to evidence, the averral–attribution distinction in source-based writing, concession, and informed choices about self-mention.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-ug: Undergraduate in-sessional support helps students build an authorial voice in assignments, evaluate sources rather than describe them, and match stance conventions to their discipline.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-pgt: Taught postgraduate support focuses on critical evaluation of literature, dialogic positioning in literature reviews and calibrated claims in dissertations.
stageEmphasis.pgr: Doctoral writers refine stance for publication: claiming contribution without over-claiming, positioning against the literature, managing self-mention and engaging expert readers.

domains.name: Rhetorical Functions
domains.summary: This domain covers recurrent rhetorical functions — defining, classifying, describing processes and structures, comparing, expressing cause and effect, exemplifying, explaining, hypothesising, recommending, summarising, narrating and evaluating — that cut across genres and disciplines. It follows the discourse approach to English for science and technology (Trimble), Mohan's knowledge framework and functional genre work (Martin and Rose; Nesi and Gardner's genre families), treating each function as a pairing of a communicative purpose with characteristic lexicogrammar and organisation. Functions are building blocks for paragraphs, sections and whole genres; teaching them through authentic disciplinary exemplars rather than decontextualised phrase lists keeps the focus on what each function achieves.
domains.learnerSummary: You will learn the common jobs that academic texts do — such as defining a term, comparing two approaches, explaining why something happens or recommending action — and the language and organisation that each job typically needs.

stageEmphasis.foundation: Foundation programmes teach the core functions (defining, classifying, describing processes, comparing, cause and effect, exemplifying) through subject content, often in science, engineering and business contexts.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional: Pre-sessional courses combine functions within extended assignments, focusing on explaining, evaluating, problem–solution and recommending in source-based writing.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-ug: Undergraduate in-sessional support targets the functions demanded by specific assignments and genre families, such as explanation, critique and case study.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-pgt: Taught postgraduate support emphasises contested and operational definitions, criterion-based evaluation, explanation of results and recommendations in dissertations and reports.
stageEmphasis.pgr: Doctoral writers mainly revisit hypothesising, defining contested constructs and explaining results within research genres.

domains.name: Reading Processes & Fluency
domains.summary: This domain covers the cognitive and linguistic foundations of academic reading: automatic word recognition, parsing of compressed academic sentences, reading fluency and volume, and the way these lower-level processes interact with background knowledge, purpose and reading load. L2 reading research finds that L2 vocabulary and grammatical knowledge are the strongest correlates of L2 reading comprehension, so the domain prioritises building the linguistic base and reading volume on which strategies depend rather than treating strategies as a substitute for them. It also addresses the practical conditions of university reading: on-screen texts, long reading lists and the legitimate, checked use of a reader's other languages.
domains.learnerSummary: You will learn how reading works, why knowing more words and reading more makes everything else easier, and how to read more fluently, cope with long reading lists, read well on screen and use your other languages wisely.

stageEmphasis.foundation: Build automaticity and reading volume through extensive reading of graded and accessible texts, alongside explicit work on parsing long sentences, background knowledge and reading purpose.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional: Diagnose each learner's vocabulary size and reading rate early, set realistic fluency targets, and introduce reading-load management and on-screen reading of authentic disciplinary texts.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-ug: Focus on coping with module reading lists, dense textbook and article prose, and strategic, transparent use of L1 resources and machine translation.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-pgt: Emphasise triage of large reading loads on compressed timelines, deliberate background-knowledge building for students changing discipline, and efficient on-screen reading.
stageEmphasis.pgr: Address sustainable reading of large literatures, realistic rate expectations for specialist and theoretical texts, and the place of plurilingual reading in research.

domains.name: Reading Strategies & Comprehension
domains.summary: This domain covers the strategies and comprehension skills that turn decoded text into usable understanding: previewing, selective reading, identifying main ideas and text organisation, tracking reference and stance, inferring, monitoring and repairing comprehension, annotating, and integrating prose with visuals. Strategy instruction has positive but variable average effects, and its benefits depend on learners having enough language knowledge to apply strategies to the text at hand. Skimming and scanning are often over-represented in materials shaped by test formats relative to the careful reading for learning and argument that dominates university study, so the domain gives priority to main ideas, structure, reference and stance, and treats speeded strategies as tools for specific purposes.
domains.learnerSummary: You will learn how to get an overview of a text, find and follow its main ideas and structure, work out what is implied and whose view is being expressed, notice when you have lost understanding and fix it, and read graphs and tables together with the text.

stageEmphasis.foundation: Prioritise paragraph and text structure, main ideas, reference tracking and textbook reading, with strategies modelled on accessible texts.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional: Integrate strategies with careful reading of authentic academic texts used in source-based assignments, and avoid test-driven over-emphasis on skimming and scanning.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-ug: Apply strategies to disciplinary textbooks and early encounters with research articles, with emphasis on stance, inference and visuals.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-pgt: Focus on research-article navigation, stance and efficient previewing of large numbers of sources.
stageEmphasis.pgr: Address fine-grained stance reading, comprehension monitoring with specialist texts and efficient navigation of research literature.

domains.name: Critical & Multiple-Text Reading
domains.summary: This domain addresses reading as evaluation and integration: reconstructing arguments, evaluating evidence and methods, surfacing assumptions and perspective, reading theoretical texts, reading across multiple sources and mapping literatures, and moving from comprehension to a reasoned response that serves writing. Critical reading is presented as questioning and evaluating rather than fault-finding, and as partly discipline-specific; the notion of critical thinking is itself contested in EAP. Research on multiple-document reading shows that attending to sources and integrating across texts are distinct skills that do not develop automatically from single-text comprehension.
domains.learnerSummary: You will learn to identify and judge the arguments and evidence in what you read, notice assumptions and perspectives, compare and connect several sources, map a body of research, and form your own reasoned response for discussion and writing.

stageEmphasis.foundation: Introduce critical reading through accessible argumentative texts, focusing on argument identification, critical questions and short reasoned responses.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional: Link critical reading to source-based writing: identifying arguments, evaluating evidence, reading for an assignment and responding critically to sources.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-ug: Apply critical reading to disciplinary sources, including multiple texts and empirical studies, with attention to assumptions and perspective.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-pgt: Emphasise methods critique, multiple-text integration and literature mapping for assignments and the dissertation.
stageEmphasis.pgr: Focus on mapping and positioning within a literature, reading theoretical texts and critiquing methods at a specialist level.

domains.name: Lecture & Academic Listening
domains.summary: Academic listening is modelled here as two interacting sets of processes: decoding, which turns the acoustic signal into words and clauses in real time, and meaning-building, which relates what has been decoded to context, discourse structure, speaker purpose and prior knowledge. The domain moves from perceptual topics (connected speech, segmentation, speech rate, accent) through lecture discourse (phases, organisational and relevance markers, main points, stance) to the settings in which students listen (live and recorded lectures, seminars, briefings, academic media), with metacognitive strategy running throughout. Listening is treated as something to be taught, not only tested, and accent variation is treated as normal in international universities rather than as deviation from a single native-speaker norm.
domains.learnerSummary: You will learn how listening to lectures and discussions works, why fast natural speech is hard to catch, and practical ways to follow the structure, key points and viewpoints of lectures, seminars and recorded talks in English.

stageEmphasis.foundation: Build decoding of connected speech and confidence with short, clearly signposted lecture extracts on accessible content, together with simple preparation routines.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional: Extend to full-length authentic lectures by varied speakers, with explicit work on lecture phases, relevance markers and main-point selection, linked to note-taking and integrated listening-to-writing tasks.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-ug: Use students' own module lectures and recordings to diagnose specific decoding or discourse problems and build independent review strategies.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-pgt: Focus on dense, fast-paced specialist lectures, seminar discussion among peers from many language backgrounds, and inferring lecturer stance on contested material.
stageEmphasis.pgr: Address research seminars, conference talks, podcasts and multi-party discussion, where speakers are specialists with varied accents who signpost less explicitly.

domains.name: Note-taking & Note-making
domains.summary: The domain treats note-taking (recording from lectures in real time) and note-making (building notes from reading and from later review) as distinct but connected practices. Following Kiewra (1985), notes serve both an encoding function, through the processing involved in taking them, and an external-storage function for later review, and the review function often matters more; the domain therefore covers selection, shorthand and format, lecture and reading notes, review, digital tools and collaboration. Claims about particular formats, or about longhand versus laptop notes, are presented with their evidential limits.
domains.learnerSummary: You will learn to take notes that capture the structure and key ideas of lectures and readings, keep a clear record of where every idea came from, and use your notes to learn, revise and write.

stageEmphasis.foundation: Establish selection, abbreviation and simple formats with short, well-structured inputs, and link notes from reading to avoiding unintentional plagiarism.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional: Develop real-time lecture notes from authentic lectures and source-tracked notes from multiple readings that feed directly into integrated writing tasks.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-ug: Work with students' own lecture and reading notes, focusing on review through self-testing and on informed choices of tools.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-pgt: Manage heavy reading loads with source-tracked, thematically organised notes that support synthesis and the dissertation.
stageEmphasis.pgr: Note-making shifts towards literature management and research records; reading notes that keep source and own words strictly apart remain central.

domains.name: Seminars & Discussion
domains.summary: Seminars, tutorials and discussion groups are where students are expected to co-construct understanding of readings and ideas in real time, and where participation is often assessed formally or informally. This domain treats discussion as negotiated, multi-turn interaction rather than a list of functional phrases: learners need to prepare substantively, find and hold turns, state and justify positions, mitigate disagreement, build on and summarise others' contributions and, at higher levels, facilitate. Participation is also shaped by anxiety, positioning and the way tutors and peers distribute the floor, so the domain addresses willingness to communicate and the conditions for participation, not only individual skill.
domains.learnerSummary: You will learn how university discussions work and how to prepare for them, get into the conversation, make and support your points, respond to others politely but critically, and help a discussion move forward, face to face or online.

stageEmphasis.foundation: Make seminar purposes and participation expectations explicit, and build reliable resources for giving views, asking questions and checking understanding through short, well-prepared, low-stakes discussions on accessible content.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional: Move from rehearsed phrases to extended negotiation of ideas from set readings, with explicit work on turn-taking, mitigated disagreement and referring to sources, often in an assessed seminar that informs progression.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-ug: Embed practice in learners' own modules, focusing on subject-specific expectations, entering fast discussions with peers who share local references, and building on others' points.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-pgt: Emphasise critical engagement with readings, citing in speech, facilitating and summarising in intensive one-year programmes where seminar contribution may be assessed from the first weeks.
stageEmphasis.pgr: Focus on research group meetings, reading groups and peer seminars on work in progress, where researchers question, critique and are questioned as emerging members of a discipline.

domains.name: Presentations
domains.summary: Academic presentations range from short assessed talks on foundation and pre-sessional programmes to conference papers, posters and research seminars at doctoral level. This domain treats the presentation as a spoken, multimodal genre designed for listeners who process information once, in real time: it needs explicit structure and signposting, visuals that support rather than duplicate speech, intelligible prosody and a delivery mode between reading a script and improvising. It gives particular attention to the interactive phases — openings and question-and-answer sessions — which research on conference presentations shows are central to how presenters engage audiences and establish credibility.
domains.learnerSummary: You will learn how to plan, design and deliver academic presentations that listeners can follow, how to talk an audience through visuals and data, and how to handle questions, from short class talks to posters and research presentations.

stageEmphasis.foundation: Build clear structure, signposting, delivery from notes and basic slide design through short, rehearsed presentations, often in groups, on accessible topics.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional: Develop individual presentations on a researched topic that use sources and data and include timed questions, often as part of progression assessment.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-ug: Support module-specific presentation tasks, including group presentations and recorded assessments, with attention to disciplinary expectations and audience.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-pgt: Focus on presenting projects and dissertation plans, explaining data, handling challenging questions and working in recorded or online formats.
stageEmphasis.pgr: Address research seminars, conference papers, posters and upgrade or progression presentations within strict time limits, framing contribution for specialist audiences and engaging productively in discussion sessions.

domains.name: Pronunciation & Fluency
domains.summary: The domain adopts the intelligibility principle (Levis, 2005): the goal is speech that listeners can understand with reasonable effort, not a native-like accent. Building on Munro and Derwing's (1995) distinction between accentedness, comprehensibility and intelligibility, priority goes to the features most likely to affect understanding in academic speaking — word stress in academic vocabulary, thought groups and prominence, intonation for discourse functions, high-functional-load segmentals — together with fluency and repair. Pronunciation is linked to listening, since perception supports production, and to the presentations, seminars and teaching in which students use it; accent is treated as part of speakers' identity rather than as an error to be removed.
domains.learnerSummary: You will learn which features of pronunciation most affect whether listeners understand you, and practise them in the speaking you do at university — presentations, seminars and explaining your work — without needing to sound like a native speaker.

stageEmphasis.foundation: Establish intelligibility as the goal, with focused work on word stress, thought groups and each learner's own highest-priority sounds.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional: Integrate prosody (thought groups, prominence, intonation) with presentation and seminar speaking, using recordings for self-analysis and listener feedback.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-ug: Provide short, targeted support for assessed presentations and technical vocabulary, usually through individual feedback.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-pgt: Focus on specialist terms, numbers and data in speech, and on fluent delivery of dense content within strict time limits.
stageEmphasis.pgr: Support conference presentations, vivas and teaching (for example as graduate teaching assistants), where prosody affects how clearly explanations come across to audiences.

domains.name: Group Work & Collaboration
domains.summary: Group projects, assessed group presentations and collaborative reports are common across disciplines, yet students often receive little guidance on how to collaborate, and multilingual students can be positioned as less competent and allocated marginal roles. This domain covers why universities assess collaboration and how groups plan and allocate work, run meetings, negotiate disagreement, write together, and document and evaluate contributions. It treats equitable participation as a shared responsibility of all group members and of course design, not as a deficit of particular students.
domains.learnerSummary: You will learn how to plan and organise group projects, run useful meetings, deal with disagreement, write together and show what you and others contributed, while making sure everyone in a multilingual group can take a full part.

stageEmphasis.foundation: Introduce the purposes of group work, simple role allocation and meeting routines through scaffolded projects with explicit ground rules and teacher monitoring.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional: Use short group projects to practise planning, meeting language and inclusive participation among students from varied backgrounds, in preparation for assessed group work on degree programmes.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-ug: Support assessed group projects with meeting management, conflict handling, collaborative writing workflows and peer evaluation of contributions.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-pgt: Address intensive, often highly multilingual group assignments in which students must quickly establish roles, resolve disagreements and document contributions for peer-moderated marks.
stageEmphasis.pgr: Focus on research-team meetings, co-authoring and documenting contributions, linking collaboration to authorship norms and professional conduct.

domains.name: Writing Process
domains.summary: Covers how academic texts are produced rather than what they look like: representing the task, generating and organising content, drafting, writing from sources, and managing time, language choice and affect across extended projects. It draws on cognitive process models (Flower & Hayes, 1981; Bereiter & Scardamalia, 1987) and L2 composing research (Zamel, 1983), which show that skilled writers plan, draft and review recursively and use writing to develop ideas. Hyland (2003) argues that process pedagogy needs to be complemented by explicit attention to genre and reader expectations, so these topics should be taught alongside PAR, ESS and the genre strands rather than as a free-standing ‘process approach’.
domains.learnerSummary: You will learn how to turn an assignment brief into a plan and a draft, how to use your reading and your other languages while you write, and how to manage longer projects and the times when writing feels stuck.

stageEmphasis.foundation: Make the process visible: task analysis, idea generation and outlining for short assignments, with plans and drafts submitted and discussed before the final text.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional: Use the extended source-based project to rehearse the full cycle under realistic deadlines, including reading-to-write, word budgeting and drafting from notes.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-ug: Apply process strategies to learners' own module assignments, with emphasis on interpreting briefs, juggling deadlines and integrating disciplinary reading.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-pgt: Compress the cycle for dense, short-turnaround master's assignments and plan ahead for the dissertation.
stageEmphasis.pgr: Treat writing as a way of thinking and as sustained practice: routines, milestones, writing blocks and plurilingual composing across a multi-year project.

domains.name: Paragraph Development
domains.summary: Covers the paragraph as the main unit through which academic writers develop and support a point: controlling ideas, support and analysis, internal coherence, closure, division, paragraph functions and the integration of sources. Paragraph scaffolds such as topic-sentence models and PEEL are useful entry points for foundation and pre-sessional writers, but expert paragraphs vary considerably (Braddock, 1974), so teaching should move learners from templates towards functional judgements about what a paragraph needs to do in its context. Coherence is better taught through information flow and logical relations than through connector lists (Crossley & McNamara, 2012).
domains.learnerSummary: You will learn how to build paragraphs that make one clear point, support it with explanation and evidence, flow logically from sentence to sentence, use sources while keeping your own voice, and connect to the rest of your text.

stageEmphasis.foundation: Build secure control of the controlling idea, support and closure, using scaffolds such as PEEL explicitly as temporary supports.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional: Shift to source-based paragraphs in which the writer's own point leads and evidence is integrated and commented on.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-ug: Diagnose paragraph-level problems in disciplinary assignments, especially description without analysis and breaks in internal coherence.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-pgt: Focus on dense, multi-source paragraphs and on flexible paragraphing that serves the argument rather than a formula.

domains.name: Essay Construction
domains.summary: Covers how an essay is built around a central argument: structure, thesis, introductions, body organisation, conclusions, relevance to the question, essay types, depth of focus, criticality, headings and titles. The essay is a major assessed genre in many humanities and social science programmes but is only one of many genre families in university writing (Nesi & Gardner, 2012), and the five-paragraph essay taught in many schools and test-preparation courses is a scaffold that does not match university essays in length, structure or source use (Caplan & Johns, 2019; Moore & Morton, 2005). Teaching should centre on argument (Wingate, 2012) and treat structural templates as means to that end.
domains.learnerSummary: You will learn how to plan and build an essay that answers the question with a clear, well-supported and critical argument, from the thesis and introduction through the body to the conclusion and title.

stageEmphasis.foundation: Introduce thesis-led essay structure with scaffolds, moving from short opinion-based essays to short source-based ones.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional: Develop extended source-based essays with a clear thesis, organised body and evaluative conclusion, and unlearn test-driven templates.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-ug: Work with disciplinary essay types, answering the specific question, choosing depth over breadth and demonstrating criticality.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-pgt: Focus on criticality, scope and argument in short, dense essays and on discipline-specific conventions such as headings.
stageEmphasis.pgr: Carry argument structure and title-writing skills into articles and thesis chapters; essays themselves are less central.

domains.name: Revising, Editing & Proofreading
domains.summary: Covers how writers improve drafts: distinguishing revision of argument and structure from sentence-level editing and surface proofreading, and the techniques, feedback sources, tools and ethical limits involved. Sommers (1980) found that inexperienced writers tend to treat revision as rewording, so teaching should put global revision and criteria-based self-assessment before editing. The value of written corrective feedback has been contested (Truscott, 1996; Ferris, 1999), but meta-analytic evidence suggests it can improve accuracy (Kang & Han, 2015); learners therefore need routines for targeted self-editing, trained peer review (Lundstrom & Baker, 2009) and critical use of tools and permitted third-party help.
domains.learnerSummary: You will learn how to improve your drafts in stages—first the argument and structure, then the sentences, then surface errors—and how to use marking criteria, classmates' feedback, digital tools and proofreaders appropriately.

stageEmphasis.foundation: Establish the difference between revising and correcting, basic self-editing routines and structured, supported peer review.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional: Build multi-draft cycles with criteria-based self-assessment, peer review and targeted editing of personal error patterns.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-ug: Apply revision strategies to module assignments and use tools and proofreading support within institutional rules.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-pgt: Focus on efficient global revision under time pressure and on critical use of editing and AI tools.
stageEmphasis.pgr: Revise long texts with reverse outlining and supervisor and peer feedback, edit for style at publication level, and understand the rules on editorial help with theses and articles.

domains.name: Information Literacy & Source Evaluation
domains.summary: Covers how scholarly knowledge is produced and published, how learners turn an assignment topic into a searchable question, how they search catalogues and databases, and how they judge whether a source is trustworthy and fit for a specific purpose. Evaluation is treated as contextual judgement, in line with the ACRL frame 'Authority Is Constructed and Contextual', rather than as checklist compliance, and lateral reading is included as an empirically grounded alternative to judging a site on its own terms. The language demands are real: generating search terms draws on vocabulary depth and disciplinary terminology, and judging a source depends on reading its genre signals and paratext.
domains.learnerSummary: You will learn how academic knowledge is published, how to find relevant sources efficiently with library tools, and how to decide whether a source is reliable enough for the job you want it to do in your work.

stageEmphasis.foundation: Distinguishing scholarly from popular sources, simple catalogue and discovery-tool searches, and basic credibility checks, including lateral reading of web sources.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional: Focusing a topic for a project, building keyword searches with synonyms and Boolean operators, evaluating sources for an extended essay, and keeping records that make accurate citation possible.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-ug: Subject databases, citation chaining from key readings, and module-specific judgements about what counts as an acceptable source.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-pgt: Efficient, documented searching for dissertations, checking venues and retractions, and legitimate access to paywalled work.
stageEmphasis.pgr: Systematic or scoping searching, comprehensive citation chaining and reproducible search records maintained across a multi-year project.

domains.name: Summarising, Paraphrasing & Quoting
domains.summary: Covers the core textual practices by which writers bring others' words and ideas into their own texts: quoting, paraphrasing and summarising, the reporting language that attributes and evaluates source content, and the signalling that keeps the writer's voice distinct from the sources'. The domain follows research suggesting that source-use problems in L2 writing are often developmental, linked to comprehension, vocabulary and an incomplete sense of why sources are used, rather than to intent to deceive (Howard; Pecorari; Shi; Keck). Instruction therefore pairs language work with purpose: learners transform sources in order to serve their own argument, and close dependence on source wording is treated as something to be taught through, not only policed.
domains.learnerSummary: You will learn how to quote, paraphrase and summarise sources accurately, how to make clear which ideas come from a source and which are your own, and how to choose language that reports other writers' ideas precisely.

stageEmphasis.foundation: Accurate quotation, basic signal phrases, summarising paragraphs and early paraphrasing, with close dependence on source wording treated as a normal stage to work through.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional: Paraphrase and summary in assessed writing, reporting verbs, voice boundaries and integration of sources in extended essays.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-ug: Disciplinary norms for quotation and citation form, summarising whole texts, and source use that serves analysis rather than display.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-pgt: Rapid, accurate summarising of research articles, evaluative reporting, and clear voice boundaries in dense, multi-source writing.
stageEmphasis.pgr: Fine control of reporting verbs, citation form and attribution in research writing, and transparent use of sources in other languages.

domains.name: Synthesis
domains.summary: Covers discourse synthesis: building a new text that integrates several sources around the writer's own organising ideas rather than summarising them one by one. The domain moves from the concept of synthesis, through tools for organising sources (matrices and thematic grouping), to the language of relating sources, identifying gaps and tensions, and writing synthesis paragraphs, and includes integrated reading- and listening-to-writing tasks. Spivey's account of synthesis as organising, selecting and connecting, together with research on integrated writing (Plakans; Plakans and Gebril; Grabe and Zhang), frames synthesis as a constructive reading–writing process rather than a set of linking phrases.
domains.learnerSummary: You will learn how to bring several sources together around your own ideas, show how they agree, differ and leave questions open, and complete tasks that combine reading, listening and writing.

stageEmphasis.foundation: Understanding synthesis versus serial summary, simple matrices built from two or three sources, and short integrated tasks.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional: Thematic grouping and synthesis paragraphs in extended essays, and integrated reading-into-writing tasks used for progression decisions.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-ug: Synthesising module readings in essays and literature review assignments, with explicit relationships between sources and, in final-year projects, identification of gaps.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-pgt: Literature reviews that group sources by theme, relate them critically and identify gaps that justify a dissertation question.
stageEmphasis.pgr: Synthesising large, contested literatures and articulating tensions and gaps that position an original contribution.

domains.name: Citation & Referencing
domains.summary: Citation is both a technical system and a rhetorical practice. This domain moves from why and when academics cite, through the mechanics of the main referencing systems (author–date, numeric and note-based), locators and reference lists, to the rhetorical functions of citation and how these vary across disciplines. Formatting is treated as learnable and checkable, ideally with reference-management tools, so that teaching time goes to the harder judgements: what needs citing, whether a cited source really supports the claim, how citation positions the writer, and what disciplinary readers expect.
domains.learnerSummary: You will learn why and when to cite, how to format citations and reference lists accurately in the system your department or journal uses, and how expert writers use citation to build and position their own arguments.

stageEmphasis.foundation: Reasons for citing, when citation is needed, and accurate author–date (or departmental) formatting for books, articles and web pages.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional: Consistent use of one system across an extended source-based assignment, with locators, reference lists and systematic accuracy checks that often feed into progression decisions.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-ug: Switching to the department's prescribed system, citing a wider range of source types, and beginning to use citation for more than attribution.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-pgt: Using citation to compare, evaluate and link sources in critical reviews and dissertations, and matching the citation norms of the discipline.
stageEmphasis.pgr: Switching between journal styles, managing large reference libraries accurately, and using citation to position a contribution within a field.

domains.name: Academic Integrity
domains.summary: Academic integrity is taught here as values and practices rather than a list of offences. The domain moves from shared values and an informed understanding of plagiarism (including the developmental status of patchwriting and the contested role of intention) to collusion, contract cheating, reuse of one's own work and research integrity, and to the procedural knowledge learners need: interpreting similarity reports, navigating policies and processes, and managing pressure without shortcuts. Rules differ between institutions and modules, so teaching centres on locating and reading the rules that apply, and similarity scores are never treated as verdicts.
domains.learnerSummary: You will learn what academic integrity means in practice, how to avoid plagiarism, collusion and other misconduct, what similarity reports do and do not show, where to get help when deadlines and pressure build up, and what your rights are if questions are ever raised about your work.

stageEmphasis.foundation: Values, a clear and non-threatening understanding of plagiarism and collusion, and where to get help, introduced early in the course.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional: Integrity in source-based writing, similarity reports as formative tools, and the policies that will govern the degree programme.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-ug: Department-specific rules on collaboration, reuse of work and lab or project data, and strategies for managing workload pressure.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-pgt: Rapid orientation to regulations, reuse of prior work, group-assessment boundaries, and integrity in dissertation research and data.
stageEmphasis.pgr: Research integrity, text recycling in theses and publications, authorship, and the codes of conduct governing research.

domains.name: Critical Thinking
domains.summary: This domain treats critical thinking as a contested, partly discipline-specific set of practices and dispositions — questioning, weighing evidence, recognising inference patterns and their limits, considering perspectives fairly and reflecting on one's own position — that can be made explicit and taught. It deliberately rejects the deficit framing that some groups of learners 'cannot think critically': differences in readiness to critique published work are treated as differences in prior schooling, assessment genres and licence to question, not as cognitive or cultural deficits. The domain supplies the reasoning that the Academic Argumentation domain turns into written and spoken argument.
domains.learnerSummary: You will learn what university tutors mean when they ask you to be 'critical', how to question and weigh evidence and reasoning, and how to notice common errors in thinking — including your own.

stageEmphasis.foundation: Make criticality concrete with familiar topics: description versus analysis, simple questions about evidence, and fair representation of different views.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional: Connect critical moves to progression tasks — source-based writing, seminars and extended projects — using the course's own criteria and exemplars.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-ug: Embed criticality in disciplinary tasks with module exemplars, especially during the first-year transition when 'be more critical' feedback first appears.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-pgt: Accelerate recalibration to master's-level expectations: evaluating research designs, competing theories and contested literatures from the first assignment.
stageEmphasis.pgr: Focus on evaluating and positioning theory, reflexivity, and the epistemological commitments of one's own research.

domains.name: Academic Argumentation
domains.summary: This domain treats argument as the organising purpose of most assessed academic writing and much academic talk: taking a position, supporting claims with evidence and explicit reasoning, anticipating and answering objections, and sequencing sub-claims into a cumulative case. Hirvela (2017) argues that L2 writing pedagogy has given argumentation less attention than its centrality warrants, and Wingate (2012) found that students often receive feedback on 'argument' without being shown what it consists of. Toulmin's model, argumentation schemes and argument mapping are offered as analytical tools rather than templates, and disciplinary variation in what counts as a good argument (Andrews, 2010) is made explicit.
domains.learnerSummary: You will learn what an academic argument is, how to build one from claims, evidence and reasoning, and how to deal fairly and convincingly with other views in writing and in discussion.

stageEmphasis.foundation: Build the concept of argument as a supported position, with simple claim–evidence–explanation links and awareness of how texts persuade.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional: Develop a sustained, qualified position in source-based essays, with counter-argument, concession and rebuttal, and transfer these moves to seminar discussion.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-ug: Adapt argument to disciplinary genres and evaluate others' arguments in readings, critiques and seminars.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-pgt: Construct extended, evidence-dense arguments in assignments and dissertations, making warrants explicit for expert readers and evaluating research arguments.
stageEmphasis.pgr: Sustain a thesis-length argument, position it within scholarly debates and defend it orally in supervision, conferences and the viva.

domains.name: Identity, Plurilingualism & Intercultural Competence
domains.summary: This domain addresses who learners are as academic language users: how writing and speaking construct identity, how plurilingual repertoires can be used strategically, how English functions as a lingua franca in international universities, and how intercultural and rhetorical differences can be understood without stereotyping. It adopts a resource rather than a deficit orientation, treats culture as dynamic, multiple and partly institutional rather than as fixed national traits, and presents contrastive rhetoric and native-speaker norms as historically influential but contested. Several topics are as much curriculum principles for teachers as content for learners, and are written so that they can serve both.
domains.learnerSummary: You will explore how academic writing and speech shape the way you present yourself, how to use all your languages as resources, and how to communicate confidently across differences without relying on stereotypes.

stageEmphasis.foundation: Build confidence in multilingual repertoires and intercultural group work as learners enter English-medium study, often for the first time.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional: Address transition, academic identity and explicit conventions alongside lingua franca interaction in multilingual cohorts.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-ug: Support inclusive group work, emerging disciplinary voice and resource-oriented participation for home and international students alike.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-pgt: Help highly international cohorts negotiate identity, intercultural collaboration and unfamiliar expectations within a short programme.
stageEmphasis.pgr: Focus on researcher identity, publishing as a multilingual scholar and positioning within global scholarly communities.

domains.name: Essay & Examination Genres
domains.summary: This domain covers the essay, examination, review and source-based genres most often assessed in foundation, pre-sessional and taught programmes, together with the genre concepts and analytic strategies learners need to handle genres they have not been explicitly taught. Each genre topic integrates component skills from the writing, sources, argument, discourse and reading strands, and describes typical purposes, stages and language; because conventions vary by discipline, department and assignment brief, every topic stresses analysis of local exemplars, briefs and marking criteria rather than a single template. The domain draws on all three genre traditions (ESP, Sydney School and New Rhetoric) and on corpus evidence about genre families in UK student writing.
domains.learnerSummary: You will learn what different kinds of academic writing are for, how they are usually organised and what language they use, and how to analyse examples and assignment briefs so that you can write new types of text that nobody has taught you.

stageEmphasis.foundation: Explanation, discussion, compare-and-contrast, problem–solution, short-answer and summary–response genres with strong scaffolding, plus the idea that texts are shaped by purpose and reader.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional: The shift from test-style opinion essays to source-based argumentative essays, critiques, annotated bibliographies and short literature reviews, with guided analysis of target-department exemplars.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-ug: Discipline-specific essays, exam essays, short answers, critiques and reflective writing, worked through real module briefs, criteria and feedback.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-pgt: Rapid adaptation to critiques, literature reviews, reflective and exam genres within a compressed year, with emphasis on criticality and independent genre analysis.
stageEmphasis.pgr: Genre analysis as an independent research skill and book reviews as early publications; most doctoral genres are covered in the Research Communication strand.

domains.name: Report & Practice-Based Genres
domains.summary: This domain covers report-based, practice-based and professional genres in which students document investigations, analyse cases, justify designs, propose projects, summarise for decision-makers, reflect on practice and write for non-academic readers. Most are discipline-specific in their sections, terminology and evidence, so each topic sets out common purposes, stages and language while stressing that lab manuals, templates, handbooks and assignment briefs override any generic model. The domain draws on genre-family research on UK student writing, analyses of particular student genres such as the lab report and the business case report, and research on reflective writing.
domains.learnerSummary: You will learn how reports, case studies, proposals, portfolios, dissertations and public-facing texts work, who reads them and what those readers need, and how to adapt to your own department's templates and expectations.

stageEmphasis.foundation: Report conventions, guided lab reports and introductory case studies and business reports in subject pathways.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional: Extended project reports, proposals and abstracts as progression assessments, with an introduction to report formats in the learners' target disciplines.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-ug: Discipline-embedded lab, design, business and case reports, placement portfolios and the final-year dissertation or project.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-pgt: Professional reports, case analyses, policy briefs, portfolios and the master's dissertation, often within a compressed timeline.
stageEmphasis.pgr: Policy briefs and public-facing writing for engagement and impact; doctoral research genres themselves sit in the Research Communication strand.

domains.name: Research Writing
domains.summary: Research Writing covers the part-genres, macrostructures and practices through which postgraduate and early-career writers report and position their own research: introductions built on CARS-type moves, literature reviews, framework and methods sections, results, discussions, conclusions, abstracts, theses and proposals. Move analyses (Swales 1990, 2004; Kanoksilapatham 2005; Yang & Allison 2003; Kwan 2006) are descriptive models to test against disciplinary exemplars, not templates, and IMRaD is dominant in experimental fields but far from universal. The domain also covers the sociopragmatic and self-regulatory work of extended research writing, such as supervision, sustaining output and writing reflexively, which Kamler and Thomson (2014) treat as both text work and identity work.
domains.learnerSummary: You will learn how research texts such as articles, dissertations and theses are organised in your field, and how to write each part so that readers can see what you did, what you found and why it matters.

stageEmphasis.pre-sessional: On postgraduate pre-sessionals, focus on reading research articles section by section, writing a short CARS-structured introduction and drafting the small-scale proposal or project that often forms part of the progression assessment.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-ug: Support final-year projects and dissertations with methods, results and discussion writing, anchored in departmental exemplars and the module's own reporting conventions.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-pgt: Treat the master's dissertation as the main site: the literature review as argument, aligning questions with methods, data commentary in results, and calibrated interpretation in the discussion.
stageEmphasis.pgr: Move to thesis macrostructure, framework chapters, claiming contribution, publication-based theses, supervision and the sustained drafting of a long document.

domains.name: Publication & Dissemination
domains.summary: Publication & Dissemination covers the genres, practices and politics through which research reaches readers and is evaluated: the publishing process, journal choice, the occluded genres around submission (cover letters, reviewer reports, responses to reviewers), conference abstracts, the doctoral viva, authorship and contributorship, public engagement and academic self-presentation. Many of these genres are hidden from novices because they are rarely published, so making exemplars and expectations visible is central to teaching. The domain also addresses the opportunities and inequities multilingual scholars meet in English-medium publishing (Flowerdew 1999; Lillis & Curry 2010) and treats them as structural issues, not individual deficits.
domains.learnerSummary: You will learn how academic publishing and research examination work, and how to write and speak in the genres that get your research reviewed, published, defended and noticed.

stageEmphasis.in-sessional-ug: Introduce academic self-presentation genres such as CVs and personal statements for postgraduate applications, and the basics of how research is published.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-pgt: Introduce the publishing process, authorship norms and conference abstracts for master's students considering research careers or publishing from dissertations.
stageEmphasis.pgr: Make this the core: journal selection, submission, peer review in both roles, the viva, authorship negotiations, engagement and impact writing, and the politics of publishing in English.

domains.name: Data Commentary & Visuals
domains.summary: Data commentary is where numerical and visual evidence becomes argument: learners must read visuals accurately, select what matters, and write or speak about it with claims calibrated to the evidence rather than exhaustive description. The domain runs from visual literacy (visual types, reading graphs and tables, recognising misleading displays) through the lexicogrammar of trends, proportions and diagrams, to the genre of data commentary and the conventions for labelling, referring to and creating visuals. IELTS Writing Task 1 is treated as a contrast case: it rewards selective description of key features, whereas university data commentary also interprets, explains, compares and qualifies.
domains.learnerSummary: You will learn to read graphs, tables and diagrams accurately, describe what they show in precise language, and use them as evidence in your own writing, including creating clear and honest visuals of your own.

stageEmphasis.foundation: Reading common graph and table types and describing trends, proportions and processes precisely, using visuals from subject modules such as business, science and engineering.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional: Moving from test-style description to data commentary that locates, highlights, interprets and qualifies, typically in an extended project or report.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-ug: Discipline-specific visual conventions in lab, project and business reports, including captions, in-text references and creating charts from learners’ own data.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-pgt: Commenting on results in dissertations with appropriately hedged interpretation, and critically evaluating visuals in sources.
stageEmphasis.pgr: Data commentary in results and discussion chapters and articles, figures designed to journal requirements, and visual argument in research presentations.

domains.name: Academic Numeracy Language
domains.summary: Academic numeracy language is the lexicogrammar and conceptual precision needed to talk and write about quantities, measurements, statistics and mathematical relations in English. Errors here are rarely ‘just language’: confusing per cent with percentage points, using ‘significant’ loosely or misplacing a unit changes the claim. The domain runs from accurate number expressions and approximation, through units and mathematical expression, to statistical vocabulary and consumer-level interpretation of statistical claims, drawing on research into statistical literacy (Gal, 2002) and risk communication (Gigerenzer et al., 2007). EAP teachers without statistical training may wish to co-teach the later topics with subject or mathematics-support colleagues.
domains.learnerSummary: You will learn to talk and write about numbers, measurements and statistics precisely, and to understand what the statistical claims in your reading do and do not show.

stageEmphasis.foundation: Number expressions, units and basic statistical terms in subject modules such as mathematics, science and business, in both speech and writing.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional: Precision and approximation in data commentary, relative versus absolute change, and the everyday versus statistical senses of key terms.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-ug: Discipline-specific notation and units, statistical vocabulary in methods and results, and reading statistical claims in sources.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-pgt: Consumer-level interpretation of p-values, confidence intervals and effect sizes in research reading and dissertations.
stageEmphasis.pgr: Accurate statistical and mathematical expression in theses and articles, following field and journal conventions.

domains.name: Multimodal Composition
domains.summary: Academic communication increasingly combines writing with images, layout, colour, sound and movement, and university assessment now includes posters, infographics, podcasts, video essays and e-portfolios. This domain treats multimodal composition as meaning-making with distinct semiotic resources (Kress & van Leeuwen, 2006), addresses the design of key academic multimodal genres (MacIntosh-Murray, 2007), and treats accessibility as a design requirement from the outset rather than an afterthought (World Wide Web Consortium, 2023). Academic expectations of argument, evidence and attribution carry over into these genres, even though the means of realising them change.
domains.learnerSummary: You will learn how images, layout and text work together, and how to design posters, infographics and digital assignments that are clear, persuasive and accessible to all your readers.

stageEmphasis.foundation: Awareness of how layout and images make meaning, developed through simple posters and short digital tasks.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional: Posters and short recorded or digital presentations as assessed work, with attention to text economy and reading paths.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-ug: Discipline-specific multimodal assessments (posters, video essays, e-portfolios) and accessible document design.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-pgt: Research posters, infographics for professional audiences and accessible dissertation formatting.
stageEmphasis.pgr: Conference posters, visual abstracts and public-engagement graphics, and accessibility in theses and publications.

domains.name: Self-Regulated Learning
domains.summary: This domain covers the knowledge and strategies that let learners direct their own academic and language development: metacognitive knowledge, the self-regulation cycle, autonomy, motivation, goal setting, time management, study techniques, language learning strategies, reflective logs, support services, wellbeing and learning content through English. It is anchored in self-regulated learning research (Zimmerman, 2002; Flavell, 1979), autonomy research (Holec, 1981; Benson, 2011) and cognitive research on durable learning (Dunlosky et al., 2013). These topics are best taught through learners' real tasks and evidence (feedback, self-test results, time logs), not as detached 'study skills'.
domains.learnerSummary: You will learn how to plan, monitor and evaluate your own learning, choose study methods that actually work, manage your time and wellbeing, and keep developing your English after your course ends.

stageEmphasis.foundation: Explicit, scaffolded introduction to independent study, time management and evidence-informed study techniques, linked to the shift from school to university-style learning.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional: Compressed work on goal setting, reflective logs and study techniques tied to weekly tasks and the progression decision, with an eye to continued development during the degree.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-ug: Embedded support at transition points (first assessments, first exam season), focusing on time management, study techniques and use of support services.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-pgt: Rapid orientation to a dense one-year programme: workload planning, independent study expectations and strategies for learning disciplinary content and language together.
stageEmphasis.pgr: Self-regulation across long, loosely structured projects: goal setting, time management, wellbeing and use of researcher development and supervisory support.

domains.name: Feedback & Assessment Literacy
domains.summary: This domain covers how learners come to understand university assessment and use feedback: assessment purposes and rules, grading systems, marking criteria, feedback literacy, acting on feedback, using written corrective feedback, seeking feedback and self- and peer-assessment. It draws on Sadler's (1989) argument that learners must come to share the assessor's concept of quality, on feedback as a support for self-regulation (Nicol & Macfarlane-Dick, 2006; Hattie & Timperley, 2007) and on student feedback literacy (Carless & Boud, 2018). On written corrective feedback, the contested evidence (Truscott, 1996; Ferris, 1999; Bitchener & Ferris, 2012; Kang & Han, 2015) should be presented honestly.
domains.learnerSummary: You will learn how university assessment works, what marking criteria and grades really mean, and how to ask for, understand and act on feedback so that each assignment improves the next.

stageEmphasis.foundation: Explicit introduction to formative and summative assessment, local grading conventions and rubrics, often the learner's first encounter with criterion-referenced coursework.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional: Intensive use of criteria, exemplars, correction codes and draft-feedback cycles leading to the progression assessment.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-ug: Interpreting disciplinary criteria and feedback on early assignments, and building feed-forward habits across modules.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-pgt: Rapid calibration to master's-level standards, where marks are often lower than learners expect and feedback windows are short.
stageEmphasis.pgr: Seeking and negotiating feedback from supervisors, peers and reviewers, and developing the evaluative judgement needed to review one's own and others' research writing.

domains.name: Exams & Timed Performance
domains.summary: This domain covers university examinations and timed performance: understanding exam formats, analysing exam questions, planning revision, writing under time pressure, approaching objective-format questions, open-book and take-home exams, oral examinations and managing test anxiety. It draws on cognitive research on retrieval and spacing (Dunlosky et al., 2013; Roediger & Karpicke, 2006), research on planning under time pressure (Ellis & Yuan, 2004), writing assessment (Weigle, 2002) and test anxiety (Putwain, 2008; Horwitz et al., 1986). Emphasis is on matching preparation and in-exam behaviour to the demands of each format rather than on generic exam tips.
domains.learnerSummary: You will learn how different university exams work, how to read exam questions precisely, how to revise so that you remember, how to write and speak well under time pressure, and how to manage exam nerves.

stageEmphasis.foundation: First experience of university-style exams in subject modules: formats, question analysis, revision planning and timed writing, often alongside content learning in English.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional: Timed writing and oral assessment as part of progression, with attention to question analysis and managing anxiety in high-stakes conditions.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-ug: Support before exam seasons: revision planning, exam essays and short answers, objective-format papers and open-book or take-home exams.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-pgt: Rapid preparation for unfamiliar formats (seen papers, take-home exams, case-based exams) within a compressed year.

domains.name: Proficiency Tests & Progression
domains.summary: This domain helps learners understand the language assessments that control access to and progression through university study: the purposes of different assessments, CEFR levels and entry requirements, the formats and constructs of academic proficiency tests, the differences between test tasks and university tasks, strategies for integrated test tasks, and pre-sessional progression assessment. It draws on language assessment theory (Bachman & Palmer, 2010; Weigle, 2002), the CEFR (Council of Europe, 2001, 2020; North, 2014) and research on test washback and on the gap between test and university writing (Green, 2007; Moore & Morton, 2005). Test formats, score requirements and visa rules change, so content is framed at the level of task types and constructs, and learners are directed to current official sources.
domains.learnerSummary: You will learn what language tests and progression assessments are for, what their scores do and do not tell you, how test tasks differ from university work, and how to prepare without letting the test narrow your learning.

stageEmphasis.foundation: Understanding entry and progression requirements and test formats, while building the broader academic literacy that tests only partly measure.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional: Central: understanding the progression assessment, how it relates to entry requirements and proficiency tests, and moving from test-oriented habits to university-oriented ones.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-ug: Addressing the transition from test preparation to disciplinary writing, especially where first-year students carry test templates into coursework.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-pgt: Rapid recalibration for master's students who entered directly with a test score and must adjust from test tasks to source-based disciplinary writing.

domains.name: Academic Culture & Expectations
domains.summary: Makes explicit how universities and disciplines are organised, what they expect of learners and how those expectations are communicated, often tacitly. The domain moves from orientation knowledge (structures, teaching formats, roles and address) through discourse-community and disciplinary awareness to perspectives (academic literacies, critical EAP, EMI and transnational education) that treat conventions as situated, variable and open to question rather than as fixed norms to be absorbed. Throughout, difficulty is framed as a mismatch between practices, not as a deficit in the learner.
domains.learnerSummary: You will learn how your university and your discipline work, what is expected of you (including things nobody says out loud), and how to adapt to these expectations and, where appropriate, question them.

stageEmphasis.foundation: Orientation to structures, teaching formats, forms of address and independent study, taught through real institutional documents at the point of need rather than in one-off information sessions.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional: Explicit comparison of prior and target practices, decoding tacit expectations in tasks and feedback, a first look at disciplinary difference, and transition support integrated into language work.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-ug: Disciplinary expectations, discourse communities and tacit criteria in the student's own modules, ideally embedded or co-taught with subject staff.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-pgt: Rapid orientation within compressed one-year programmes, disciplinary knowledge-making for students changing field, and academic literacies perspectives that help students interpret feedback.
stageEmphasis.pgr: Doctoral expectations of independence, disciplinary epistemologies, the researcher's place in research communities, and critical perspectives on English-medium scholarship.

domains.name: Academic Pragmatics & Correspondence
domains.summary: Covers the sociopragmatic and pragmalinguistic resources learners need to interact with staff and peers outside the core academic genres: politeness and face, requests, apologies and accounts, emails, office hours, formal institutional statements, forum posts, channel choice and acknowledgements. Interlanguage pragmatics research shows that pragmatic competence does not keep pace with grammatical development without attention, and that staff judge messages on perceived politeness and clarity as well as accuracy. Norms are presented as variable across institutions, countries and individuals; the aim is informed, context-sensitive choice, not one correct formula.
domains.learnerSummary: You will learn how to write emails, make requests, apologise, take part in meetings and online discussions, and write formal statements in ways that are clear and appropriate for the people you are communicating with.

stageEmphasis.foundation: Core forms of address, request and apology language, and email structure, practised on real tasks such as contacting a tutor or reporting an absence.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional: Calibrating politeness to power, distance and imposition; email and office-hour rehearsal for the destination institution; forum participation on the course VLE.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-ug: Applying pragmatic knowledge to real situations as they arise (extensions, feedback tutorials, assessed forums, extenuating circumstances claims), with attention to local norms.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-pgt: Efficient, well-judged correspondence and meetings within a compressed timeline, including requests for references and dissertation-related contact.
stageEmphasis.pgr: High-imposition requests to supervisors, external researchers and gatekeepers, multichannel professional communication, and acknowledgements in theses and articles.

domains.name: Digital Scholarship Tools
domains.summary: Academic work is mediated by digital tools (learning platforms, word processors, reference managers, shared documents, machine translation and automated writing evaluation) whose effective and ethical use is rarely taught explicitly. This domain treats these tools as part of academic literacy practices rather than as separate technical skills (Lea & Jones, 2011), emphasising critical and transparent use: tools support but do not replace learners’ judgement, their outputs must be checked, and their permitted use is set by institutional policy. Because products change quickly, topics are framed around transferable functions and decisions rather than named applications.
